collection_summary: This instance is a curated, source-defined ground truth listing the 18 US presidents who held office for any portion of the 20th century (1 January 1901 through 31 December 2000), as listed in the lone wikitable of the Wikipedia 'List of presidents of the United States' master article. For each president the staged row records Term Start Year (year of inauguration, verbatim from the source's Term cell begin date), Term End Year (year of leaving office, regardless of cause, verbatim from the source's Term cell end date), Party (Republican or Democratic — both party values that appear in this window), and Vice President(s) (the rowspan-expanded set of named VPs across all the president's terms, alphabetized and semicolon-delimited within the cell, with Vacant-interval markers filtered out). The 18-row universe runs from William McKinley (1897-1901, whose 20th-century overlap is January 1 to September 14, 1901 before his assassination) through Bill Clinton (1993-2001, whose 20th-century overlap is the full 1993-2000 plus the first 20 days of 2001); George W. Bush's term began January 20, 2001 and is therefore outside the 20th-century window.
source_coverage_notes:
Roles:
- source_urls[0] (List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States): universe + filter + value (defines the canonical president set, supplies the per-row President name, Term Start Year, Term End Year, Party, and Vice President(s) cells from the master wikitable). The master table contains 1 wikitable with 84 rows total (1 header + 83 data rows covering all 47 US presidents from George Washington to the current incumbent); the 18 staged rows are exactly the presidents whose Term cell overlaps the 20th century.

Single-source Tier B instance. The Wikipedia master article is the canonical compilation of US presidential terms. No per-president article is used because every cell in this schema is sourced from the master table's rowspan-expanded structure: Name, Term Start Year, Term End Year, and Party are all single-cell-per-president; Vice President(s) is multi-cell-per-president via rowspan and is collapsed into a semicolon-delimited cell at staging time.
decision_log:
Candidate card (per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: Pass. Universe (US presidents who served any portion of 1901-2000) is fully source-defined via the cited master article and the explicit temporal filter; partition rule (per president) is source-defined; per-row attribute cells are all source-defined via the master wikitable. Table is LLM-knowable for a pre-2025 cutoff: every 20th-century US president is canonical knowledge; the calibration challenge is on the less-frequently-recalled cells like Hoover's VP (Charles Curtis) and Coolidge's VP (Charles G. Dawes), and on the multi-VP succession sequences (FDR's three VPs in order, Nixon's two VPs reflecting the Agnew resignation). Row count (18) is comfortably above the 10-row gate.
- Seed/provenance: VERBATIM seed #18 from `example_questions.txt` ('20th-century US presidents × attrs'). One of the 7 previously-untouched seeds in `example_questions.txt`; the others (#6, #8, #12) fail the fast viability gate at strict reading, #13 has weak source-grounding, and #16/#17 remain untouched for future picks.
- Category: multi_attribute_projection (gap 2 → gap 1; brings the category to 7 of 8 target — first multi_attribute_projection to approach saturation behind set_operation at 7 of 8 and set_filter at 4 of 5) primary; temporal (gap 3) secondary because the Term Start / Term End year columns give a meaningful 1897-2001 axis. Per references/artifact-contract.md, multi_attribute_projection pairs canonically with operation_type=projection; the db_analog 'SELECT president, term_start, term_end, party, vice_presidents FROM us_presidents WHERE term_overlaps_period(1901-01-01, 2000-12-31)' is the canonical multi-column projection over a temporally-filtered universe.
- Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, single source URL; gt_construction = manual_wikipedia; source_count = 1.
- Expected shape: 18 rows × 5 columns; PK = President.
- Domain: History/Politics — matches the existing precedent set by `us_presidents_count_by_birth_state` (registered + re-staging), which is also filed under History/Politics. Both instances are about US presidents but they're structurally complementary: the existing instance is `aggregation` (count of presidents grouped by birth state), this instance is `multi_attribute_projection` (per-president biographical attributes). Together they fill out the History/Politics subdomain.
- Risks/adaptation: the 'served any portion of the 20th century' filter is a curator-imposed temporal interpretation of seed #18's 'twentieth-century US presidents' phrasing; the alternative 'whose term started in the 20th century' reading would exclude McKinley and yield 17 rows. Both readings are above the 10-row gate; the more-inclusive 'served any portion of' reading is chosen because it matches the natural-language meaning of 'twentieth-century US presidents' (any president alive and in office during the 20th century) and includes McKinley's iconic transitional presidency (which spanned the 19th-to-20th century boundary and culminated in the September 1901 assassination that elevated Theodore Roosevelt to the presidency). The Multi-VP cells require alphabetization within the cell rather than chronological — alphabetization is the standard convention applied to FutureLearn's 12 founding partners, XuetangX's 2 founders, etc. (see `major_b2c_online_learning_platforms` curation.json::normalization_decisions for the precedent). The alternative chronological ordering would expose VP-sequence knowledge but is non-standard for this benchmark.
- Decision: Stage.

Why verbatim seed: seed #18 is one of the 7 previously-untouched seeds in example_questions.txt and was the highest-rubric ★★★ tied pick on the 2026-05-11 picker snapshot (tied with an original gap-4 instance). The user chose seed #18 over the original gap-4 alternative; the seed-first principle plus the multi_attribute_projection-to-saturation effect makes #18 a strong fit.

Why History/Politics rather than Politics/Government: precedent. The existing `us_presidents_count_by_birth_state` instance is filed under History/Politics, and matching that classification preserves cross-instance consistency. A counter-argument is that Politics/Government is already at 5 instances (well-represented) while History only has 1 instance (the count-by-birth-state precedent), so adding a second History instance brings History to 2 and keeps Politics at 5. Either way, History/Politics is the operative label.

Why single-source rather than multi-source-per-president: the master Wikipedia article supplies all 5 cells per row without ambiguity (Name, Term Start, Term End, Party, VP(s) are all in the master table). Adding per-president articles would yield additional attributes like Home State, Predecessor, Successor, or Manner of Leaving Office, but at the cost of multi-source complexity. The single-source 5-col design is a tighter source-defined claim. The trade-off is captured in open_questions.

Category ↔ operation_type pairing: query_category=multi_attribute_projection pairs canonically with operation_type=projection. The 4-attribute SELECT per row (Term Start, Term End, Party, VP) over a temporally-filtered universe is the canonical multi-attribute projection structure.

Why not a Home State or Manner-of-Leaving column: per the source-rigor principle, columns should source-ground cleanly from the cited URL set. Home State (state of residence at election) is in per-president Wikipedia article infoboxes, not in the master list, so adding it would require multi-source. Manner of Leaving Office is partially in the master table's Term cell footnotes (e.g., '[e]' on McKinley/Harding/FDR/Kennedy for death-in-office and '[h]' on Nixon for resignation), but the source footnote codes are inconsistent across rows and would require curator interpretation to map to clean categorical values. Keeping the schema to 5 cols all source-grounded from the master table is the cleaner staging choice; a v2 with multi-source enrichment is captured in open_questions.
normalization_decisions: Universe definition: the staged universe is the 18 US presidents whose presidential term overlaps the 20th century, defined as the calendar period 1 January 1901 to 31 December 2000 inclusive. The 'overlap any portion' interpretation is preferred over the stricter 'term started in 1901-2000' reading because the former matches the natural-language sense of 'twentieth-century US presidents' (any president alive and in office during the 20th century) and includes William McKinley, whose 20th-century portion of his presidency (January 1 to September 14, 1901, when he died from gunshot wounds sustained September 6) ended with his successor Theodore Roosevelt's ascension. Specifically: McKinley qualifies (Sept 1901 death within 1901); Clinton qualifies (term 1993-2001, 20th-century portion is all of 1993-2000); George W. Bush is excluded (term started January 20, 2001, after the 20th century ended on December 31, 2000). Name normalization: each president's name is taken from the master table's Name column with the (birth-death) parenthetical suffix stripped (e.g., source 'William McKinley (1843–1901)' → staged 'William McKinley'; source 'Bill Clinton (b. 1946)' → staged 'Bill Clinton'). Wikipedia's preferred form is used for each president — 'Bill Clinton' rather than 'William Jefferson Clinton', 'Jimmy Carter' rather than 'James Earl Carter Jr.', 'Theodore Roosevelt' rather than 'Theodore Roosevelt Jr.'. Footnote markers like '[19]' or '[73]' on the Name cell are stripped. Term Start Year normalization: 4-digit integer, the year component of the source's Term cell begin date (e.g., source 'March 4, 1897 – September 14, 1901' → Term Start Year 1897). Term End Year normalization: 4-digit integer, the year component of the source's Term cell end date (e.g., same example → Term End Year 1901). For inauguration boundary cases: McKinley's Term Start Year is 1897 (verbatim from the source), even though his 20th-century overlap begins in 1901; Clinton's Term End Year is 2001 (verbatim from the source), even though his 20th-century overlap ends on December 31, 2000. Party normalization: 2-value categorical (Republican or Democratic). In the staged 18-row universe, all 18 presidents are Republican or Democratic; no third-party president held office in the 20th century (Theodore Roosevelt ran on the Progressive 'Bull Moose' ticket in 1912 but his 1901-1909 presidency was Republican; the staged Party cell reflects the party at the time of office, not subsequent affiliations). Distribution: Republican 11 (McKinley, Theodore Roosevelt, Taft, Harding, Coolidge, Hoover, Eisenhower, Nixon, Ford, Reagan, George H. W. Bush) and Democratic 7 (Wilson, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Truman, Kennedy, Lyndon B. Johnson, Carter, Clinton). Vice President(s) normalization: the cell is a semicolon-delimited list of all named individuals who served as VP during that president's full presidency, alphabetized within the cell. 'Vacant' interval entries from the source (e.g., 'Vacant through March 4, 1925' for Coolidge's first term before Charles Dawes, 'Vacant after November 21, 1899' for McKinley after Hobart's death) are filtered out because vacant periods are not vice-presidential appointments. Three rows have multi-VP cells reflecting either succession events or multi-term presidencies: (1) William McKinley 'Garret Hobart; Theodore Roosevelt' (Hobart 1897-1899 until his death, then vacant until Roosevelt's 1901 inauguration); (2) Richard Nixon 'Gerald Ford; Spiro Agnew' (Agnew 1969-1973 until his October 1973 resignation, then vacant briefly, then Ford 1973-1974 under 25th Amendment confirmation); (3) Franklin D. Roosevelt 'Harry S. Truman; Henry A. Wallace; John Nance Garner' (Garner 1933-1941, Wallace 1941-1945, Truman January-April 1945 until FDR's death — the largest VP count in US history because of FDR's four-term presidency). All other 15 presidents have exactly 1 VP.
open_questions: 1. Whether to widen the schema to multi-source (master article + 18 per-president Wikipedia articles) to add Home State, Predecessor, Successor, and Manner of Leaving Office columns. This would yield a richer 7-9 col schema but at the cost of multi-source complexity (source_count would jump from 1 to 19) and per-president-article infobox heterogeneity that has caused multi-cycle audit arcs in similar multi-source instances (see `major_b2c_online_learning_platforms` 10-cycle arc, `landmark_us_supreme_court_decisions_by_chief_justice` 11-cycle arc). The current single-source design prefers source-rigor over schema-richness. 2. Whether the 20th-century filter should be 'term started in 1901-2000' (excludes McKinley, 17 rows) or 'served any portion of 1901-2000' (current design, 18 rows). The two readings differ only in whether McKinley is included; both clear the 10-row gate. The 'served any portion' reading is preferred because it matches the natural-language sense of 'twentieth-century US presidents' and includes McKinley's iconic transitional presidency. 3. Whether the Vice President(s) cell should be alphabetized (current design, matching the FutureLearn 12-founding-partners precedent) or chronologically ordered (would expose VP-succession-sequence knowledge for the 3 multi-VP rows). The chronological ordering would test additional LLM calibration (e.g., does the model know that FDR's VPs went Garner → Wallace → Truman in that order, not alphabetical Truman/Wallace/Garner). A v2 could adopt chronological ordering as the cell convention but at the cost of cross-instance inconsistency. 4. Whether to include the Vice Presidents themselves (Theodore Roosevelt 1901-1909 as VP under McKinley before becoming president 1901, etc.) as separate rows — i.e., 'persons who held the presidency or vice-presidency in the 20th century' instead of 'persons who held the presidency in the 20th century'. The current design narrows to the presidency only; a v2 could widen to include the 23 VPs of the 20th century. 5. Whether McKinley's Term End Year (1901) should reflect the actual end-of-presidency date (September 14, 1901, the date he died) or the year of his inauguration's next-term-end date (March 4, 1901 had he completed his second term — but he didn't). The current design uses 1901, the verbatim year from the source's '– September 14, 1901' end date, which is the year of his death.
